title: Andrea Roberts - Designing a Roguelike for People Who've Never Played Roguelikes
speaker: Andrea Roberts
talk_title: Designing a Roguelike for People Who've Never Played Roguelikes
description:
This talk is from the 2020 virtual Roguelike Celebration:
https://roguelike.club/event2020.html

Andrea is the co-founder of Wonderbelly Games, a tiny indie studio that just released their critically acclaimed debut: a bouncy physics-based roguelike called Roundguard. Before that, she spent a decade in Narrative, UX, and Game Design at Microsoft. She splits her days between making games and raising her four-year-old, and on any given afternoon, Andrea may be a princess, a triceratops, or a triceratops-princess.

In this talk she discusses how her team approached making Roundguard accessible to an audience that's unfamiliar with roguelikes -- handling the difficulty curve, presenting player options around difficulty, modifying tone and friendliness to create a feeling of chill -- while still sticking strong to the principles at the heart of roguelikes that make them so special.

Find her on Twitter: https://twitter.com/TanookiFruit
Roundguard: https://store.steampowered.com/app/848030/Roundguard/

Triceratopss or any other. We have a video. >> Hi, I am going to talk about designing
a Roguelike for people who have never played a Roguelike.
Earlier this year, we shipped Roundguard. Roundguard is a bouncy Dungeon Crawl Stone
Souper with pin ball physics where you shoot your character into a dudgeon and survive against the
constant threat of permadeath trying to make to the bottom of a procedurally generates dudgeon.
When we started making the game, we knew we needed to make round work for people new to Roguelikes.
We had this inspiration from peggle which is a casual game with broad audience. We wanted those
people to find the game and feel welcome in it. We knew a lot of them may not be comfortable with
Roguelikes. Also, when we started making the game and we know their audience is there but they are
less comfortable with Roguelike fundamentals than the PC audience. On top of that, I have a very
personal reason and that was, you know, before we started working on Roundguard about a year before,
I had become a new mom. And my experience with gaming really changed at that point.
You know, I really loved these big epic RPGs. I played a ton of strategy simulation games
and I was having a really hard time finding the time to do that anymore. That's when I found
Roguelikes. I wasn't really familiar with the genre before but I learned I could get that real
strategic doubt I was looking for in the short play sessions. Sit down, play for 35-45 minutes,
die and then stop. If it took me another week or so before I found the time again to get a play
session in, I wasn't coming in in the middle of a big epic storyline or inventory management mess. I
had to remember I was starting fresh. I love the feeling and wanted to bring that to more people.
So, I knew my goal was to make a Roguelike that captures the heart of the genre while making it
accessible to folks who don't play Roguelikes which begs who is is heart of the genre?
I see this as serving the goal of learning. Real, true deep learning where players are
discovering for themselves the underlying rules of the games that they are practicing and failing
because failure is an important part of learning but they are continuing to hone their mastery and
understanding of these systems so that they can improvise in the face of whatever the generator
shows at them. My initial assumptions about what I want to do to make a Roguelike more accessible
to a broader audience might have been make the game easier or more tutorials to get them through
the game. Looking at it as this heart of learning, you know, I really needed to protect that
part of the experience so that reframed my goal to say I am trying to encourage learning and more
than anything, I am trying not to interfere with learning. I don't want to interrupt the player
and give them the answer when they are about to figure it out. I want to have faith in people
that they can learn and give them space to experiment and I don't want to give them a
false sense of progress with some kind of grain to win mechanics. I want them to come away at the end
of the experience feeling like they beat the game because of the learning that they made themselves.
OK. What did we to make Roundguard more accessible to people who were not used to Roguelikes?
We tried to identify those assumptions that came along with the genre and the
things that maybe these players were not comfortable with and didn't know to expect.
We thought about how we were pacing the complexity for them as they were getting into
the game. We needed to keep the tone welcoming and encouraging throughout and we had the player
choices for how to tune the experience and that challenge level for themselves.
First up, identifying genre assumptions. By this, I mean that the source of things you say.
Everybody knows this coming into a Roguelike. Because Roguelikes are about learning, so much
of that difficulty is in what you already have, you know, you are understanding in your head.
And so, as players come in who are really comfortable with Roguelikes, they
already have a lot of things they know to expect. That means for players who are new to the game,
the game is going to be harder for them because there are all these things they
haven't learned by playing at the Roguelikes. I wanted to be really Cognizant of that.
What were some of the assumptions we started with? Well, you know, players, and enemies trade damage
when they come into collision and are in range. There are complications to that behavior but
that's the basics. Of course, health management over time is really important. You are taking
damage from all these enemies. We are never healing you up at the end of a turn or board.
You need to be paying attention to our health and the health opportunities on the board and making
sure you are balancing that all all your actions. We thought these were basic things to learn and we
thought something that we can just drop people in the system and they will figure it out quickly but
it turned that was an assumption. As we started with the first player test, we had an early
procedural demo and we let people get in and were seeing challenges with the basic concepts.
When you think about it, it is not really that surprising. There are lots of games out there
where the player is actually avoiding most of the damage coming from enemies.
Long form health management isn't important in a lot of games. In a lot of games you are healed
up after every encounter or major points. It is not something that everybody is used to thinking
about. We made a slight tweak to our demo and here is a screenshot of the earliest prototypes.
So we stilled -- still dropped in and introduced this tutorial character the book keeper. She pops
in and says when you hit a monster, they hit you back so heal up with the red health potions over
there. That helped bring more folks on board. We were able to get past this initial step.
There were still people struggling and there is a lot going on when you drop somebody right into
a Roguelike. You know, right now, there is, you know, I have got my hero and I have got my skills
and there are different monster types because the demo experience was procedural like
depending on when you are playing on new monster types coming in with different status effects and
all kinds of complications. It was overwhelming for a lot of people and they were not really able
to process the information. I needed to recognize that for some people, like these were real
fundamentals they needed to learn before they can get past the focus of the game and needed complete
focus to understand that. We finally made a very, you know, step-by-step tutorial. It is short.
Right at the beginning of the game where we really walk you through, hey, enemies have attack,
when you hit them, they hit you back, you will take damage and heal up with health potions.
And once we saw people get through this quick tutorial we saw everybody getting through the
basic concepts and they were able to move through the game and get into the deeper systems.
After this quick tutorial or at the end there is an introduction to skill. We teach you one
skill from each class and tells you skills are really important and drop you into the system
and let you play around with it. It turns out in Roundguard skills are really important. They
are really the most important way for you to deal with that health damage tradeoff.
For a lot of players, you know, that little skill was great. Playing with skills is a lot of fun.
They got into it and never needed help. We still saw a few people struggling with the concept.
Built into the system was a little safety net. We are watching you. If you go for a couple boards
and are not using your skills then that little tutorial character pops up and says remember
skills. They are super important. They are the difference between life and death in this game.
I was looking for things new players needed so they could be at the same base level as everybody
else and enjoy the rest of the system. At first I worried I was spoiling a learning opportunity
but I learned everybody coming in with the expectations from other roguelikes they know
the concepts. This isn't the fun part of the game. The fun part is seeing the rest of the systems and
how they unfold. And then drop them into the game system but keep an eye on them and for players
struggling we built in a couple safety Nets. Key to all of this is the testing of assumptions.
Now players need to learn about status effects and adding new bash behaviors and all of this. --
behaviors. This possibility space is exciting but it be overwhelm and that can be a turn
off for some players. They can miss important concepts in all that overload. We really need
to think about how we wanted to balance rolling out that complexity through that experience.
We did the natural choice of the deeper you go the more you encounter complications.
Because of the structure of a Roguelikes you will see the beginning part most. You will die, repeat
and keep going over the first tor territory and I want to make sure that territory stays fresh
for experienced players but for the new players coming in isn't completely overwhelming them.
To solve this challenge, we ended up holding on to some of these complications
and unlocking them as we saw players provering they understand the game and are ready for more.
As players got deeper into the dudgeon, and proved they were able to survive, when you make
it halfway through one, you unlock this and it is key to the system. It appears on every board.
As you beat the act 2 boss you unlock chaos rooms and changes how the procedural generator builds
out the map. Once you beat the final game then you start to unlock relics which let
you change the fundamental rules of the game. As you keep going further and further into the game,
we keep pushing more experiences back into the generator to really grow and
complicate the game. We want to make sure as we push new things into the generator
it wasn't just about making the game harder. We didn't want to feel like you were punished
but it is more about recognizing you have all of the tools. We see you and want to give you more
opportunities and more complicated experiences to express what you have learned. Rolling out
complexity. We held back some complications. We checked in on players to see they were proving
they had learned enough and they could handle more and we added more to the procedural generator.
Throughout the game we want to keep this welcoming and am -- encouraging tone. We have a cute and
cheerful look to the game. A broad sense of humor and cast. One of the challenges is permadeath.
For a lot of players who are not comfortable with Roguelikes permadeath is a really scary word.
But that feeling of failure and need to repeat is a core part of the experience. How do we make
people feel like it is OK to fail, really, is a core part of the learning experience?
One of the things we did was in our narrative structure of the game. At a meta level, Roundguard
takes place in this sort of play/theater framing. There is a curtain and host who
show up and an audience who clap when they do well. When you die, the host comes up
with the message of no worries, just a bad run and we will reset the stage and get you started over.
We want to lower the stakes for you. This isn't a life or death moment. This is just practice
and a bunch of people having fun in a theater. At the death moment you have an opportunity
to win a token you can take forward with you on your next run. It is not really run changing
but it is a little something to give you, you know, an idea of how you might strategize
and more than anything it is sense of hope that the next run can go different.
We launched with these elements. I really hate the feeling of losing all of my progress. The thing
was, it is like, you haven't lost your progress. So we want to think about how could we celebrate
what you have done so far in the game. We did a UI overhaul where we put up front and center every
run where you put up all the unlocks. Here are the relics you unlocked and mastered and here is
how far you have come in your progression on score. We want to remind players that there
is so much we have learned along the way. Being opening is telling players it is OK to fail. We
tried to lower the stakes and encouraging players to try again by giving them a little something
and we try to celebrate their accomplishments and remind them of how much they have accomplished.
Finally we want to give the player the choices on how they want to tune the game. Difficulty
is subjective. For new players these foundational concepts are very basic to Roguelikes and may be
challenging to them and they may need to practice. Some players are coming in wanting a relaxing game
to chill with and others want an intense challenge and people have different capabilities and
interest they want to engage with and as a designer I can't predict all of these and give you
the perfect game but I can give you tools so you can make the game more like what it is you want.
One of the ways we gave players choices is a basic way many games do and we give you
three different classes. The warrior, Rogue and the wizard. We specifically kept in mind
the types of players I wanted these classes to target. The warrior is the simplest and
the most straightforward. He is a great intro character and smashes his face into things and
gets things done and the Rogue is more about control and precision and then the wizard
really introduces more complex skills that are difficult to control and creates new challenges.
I thought everybody had these base assumptions about what each RPG class/archetype is like but
of course that turned out to be an assumption. You know, I was seeing people play in the game
who say started with the warrior, and we put him front and center as an intro character
but, you know, they played that first experience and came away saying this game isn't complicated
enough for me. They didn't realize they made that choice in picking that class.
So recently in an update, we tried to clarify that and we just added a
little complexity meter so you understand that this is a choice that you are making.
Throughout the game, we have got this score system. Early on when you were playing Roundguard
you are thinking about survival. It is, you know, kill the monsters, keep your health up and survive
to the bottom and you can beat the game. But as you start to really get into the game and
understand the scoring system you learn that you could beat the game better with a better score
and the scareb is really key to this. It moves around peg to peg between each shot and once
you hit it anything you hit afterwards the points are multiplied. A good score run becomes all about
chasing this. As you think about chasing the scareb it is like how do I hit it with a skill
before hitting the rest of the board? Sometimes it goads you into press your luck choices where
it is like I really should be going for this health over here but I got to get the scarab.
As you start the play that way, the game naturally becomes more difficult without us doing changes to
the game system because of the extra complications and weird places that the scarab can take you.
Finally, when you beat the game, you start to unlock these relics.
Every relic touches on a core system of the game and changes the fundamental rules.
For example, here is the relic of instinct. Heroes are shielded if you launch within two seconds.
There are relics that change how status effects work, how enemies respond, how the
map is generated and how gravity works and all the different relics as you click them you can layer
on as many as you want. There is also a key relic. The mercy relic is for people who are struggling
with the challenge level of the game. Gold sources are reduced and you can still beat the game.
We wanted the mercy relic to be there as a tool for players who are feeling frustrated and wanted
training wheels to let them get more comfortable with the game. We found it was helpful for kids
and we wanted to make sure the communication around the mercy relic was respectful and
people never felt like they were less than for never chosen to take on the mercy relic.
This is one of my favorite pieces of fan feedback we got in which this kid says
I rescued the king, meaning beat the game, and mastered mercy. I love that pride that is there.
That was important that, you know, I didn't want people to feel like we were talking down to them
by offering them the nursey relic. However, in the wild, we saw some people having some trouble
with the communication around the mercy relic. I watched streamers who came in and when they
first found the mercy relic they found more potion and better stats and equipped it but
without understanding they were putting on easy mode. So I worry they are going to come away with
the wrong understanding of what the game can be. After some debate, we added in this update
the word easy mode up front. You know, I want to make sure we are staying respectful about our
communication but extremely clear so people know when they are making that choice. I am giving the
players choices. It is about understanding our balance is never going to be perfect so we will
give them tools to control it themselves. And you know, I wanted to keep the tone respectful
throughout. Respectful of whatever challenge level you are looking for. I also learn it is important
to be clear so people understand when they are making a choice and what that choice means.
So we did all these things to make Roundguard more accessible to players who were not
comfortable with Roguelikes and how did we do? We heard a lot of stores from not a gamers.
My name is not a gamer. Her first experience with a Roguelike and she screamed with joy
when things went well for her in the game. We heard from Roguelike skeptics.
It is an amazing addictive game and I don't normally like pebble.
We heard from families. I love my son is learning about stats and RPG elements. It has
been our family's quarantine savior. My wife and son play it every morning. My 8 year old,
I take turns with my 8 year old. We played for three hours and haven't beaten the act 2 boss
but it is such a chill and fun game. We heard so many stories from families who have been
playing together and having a lot of fun. That was really something that was exciting for me.
Why is this worth it? I am definitely not here making the argument that everybody needs to, you
know, make a less complicated or more accessible Roguelike. I love the Roguelikes that exist out
there but I think we all agree Roguelikes are awesome and bringing that love to more people
is a great thing. And it turns out that Roguelikes have a ton of utility for people who maybe aren't
familiar with them. You know, like I said, as a parent, I found this real appreciation for their
short play session. I heard from a lot of parents how much they were enjoying for their kids this
process of, you know, the repetition and practice and learning that came along with the Roguelike.
And really this, you know, this joy of learning is such an important goal to share with people.
We have this really fun experience a couple weeks ago on our steam forum. Someone came in
and was asking questions about the game and wanted answers and we gave them a few but we also talked
to them a little bit about our philosophy of you can learn this stuff once you try a little bit
more come back and tell us how it goes. They did come back and a few days later and said
I admit the more I play the game the more I understand how much fun it is to discover. I
really love this story. This is success to me. Roguelike designers and players and were
gauged in this dialogue about the process of learning. We are experimenting with the joy
of exploration and finding comfort in failure and the grit to keep practicing. These are beautiful
values we are all spreading as a Roguelike community and I think that's really special.
